planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, since this bush bean rots quickly in cold, wet ground.

directions: This compact bush bean produces small, glossy, jet-black seeds that cook down into the smooth, creamy pot of black beans central to Cuban frijoles negros and the island's classic rice-and-beans pairing, moros y cristianos. Let pods dry fully on the plant until they rattle before shelling, then cure the seed a further week or two indoors to prevent mold in storage. Unlike the larger black turtle bean, the Cuban strain was selected over generations by island growers for a shorter, more compact plant habit and an earlier dry-down suited to warm, humid lowland growing seasons. Keep rows weed-free and avoid overhead watering once pods begin to dry, to reduce fungal staining of the seed coat.

planting.note: Plant rooted suckers (pups) in deeply dug, manure-rich soil once nighttime lows reliably stay above 60 F, since Topocho has little cold tolerance.

directions: Topocho is a short, thick-fingered cooking plantain long grown in the lowland river valleys of western Venezuela, especially around the Lake Maracaibo basin in Zulia, where it is fried into tajadas and patacones at nearly every meal. The squat bunch carries fewer, blockier fingers than a Harton plantain, and the pulp stays starchier and lower in sugar even at full ripeness, which is why it is almost always cooked rather than eaten raw. Give the mat-forming rhizome constant soil moisture and heavy monthly feeding through the growing season, and remove all but one or two follower suckers per mat so energy goes into the fruiting pseudostem. Harvest the bunch when the top fingers begin to round out and the tips yellow, then ripen it off the plant in a shaded, humid spot.
sources: Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Agricolas (INIA) Venezuela

planting.note: Set out sword suckers in deep, fertile, well-drained ground once nighttime temperatures hold above 60 F, and stake tall bunches against wind as fruit swells.

directions: Dominico Harton is the workhorse plantain landrace of the Andean foothill valleys of Colombia and western Venezuela, prized as intermediate in size between the small Dominico type and the large Harton type, with a tall, vigorous pseudostem and a long bunch of big, angular fingers. Farmers favor it for steady year-round bearing and a thick peel that resists bruising in transport to market, where it is sold green for frying into patacones and tostones or left to ripen for sweeter baked and boiled preparations. Plant it in deep, well-manured soil with reliable irrigation through dry spells, and thin each mat down to one main stem plus a single follower sucker to keep bunches large. Protect the shallow root mat from competing weeds, since the tall stature makes mature plants prone to toppling once a heavy bunch forms.
sources: Universidad Nacional de Colombia Platano Research Program

planting.note: Germinate whole husked nuts on their sides in a nursery bed or large pot, then transplant the sprouted seedling to its permanent coastal spot once several leaves have formed.

directions: Jamaica Tall is the traditional dooryard and plantation coconut of Jamaica, grown for generations for both copra and fresh drinking nuts before becoming best known as one of the two parents of the lethal-yellowing-resistant Maypan hybrid. The palm grows to full tree height with a long juvenile period, taking several years before its first bunches of large, thick-husked nuts appear, and it remains more vulnerable to lethal yellowing disease than its dwarf-crossed offspring. Site it in deep, sandy, well-drained soil within reach of coastal salt spray and wind, and keep young palms watered through dry spells until the deep root system is established. The mature nuts yield sweet water and thick, oily meat favored for fresh eating and traditional Jamaican coconut drops and oil.
sources: Jamaica Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries Coconut Industry Board
Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Coconut Genetic Resources

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger passes; this bush bean was bred for reliable dry-down even under hot, humid lowland conditions.

directions: Tio Canela 75 is a cinnamon-red bush bean bred in the 1990s at Honduras's Escuela Agricola Panamericana (Zamorano) specifically to give Central American smallholders a dry bean with strong field resistance to common bacterial blight and bean golden mosaic virus, two diseases that had been devastating local harvests. Its name, meaning 'Uncle Cinnamon,' comes from the warm reddish-brown seed coat, and the variety spread quickly from Honduran extension programs into home gardens and small farms across the region because of its reliable yields even in a difficult season. Grow it exactly as you would any bush dry bean, sowing directly into warm soil and keeping the ground evenly moist until flowering, then easing off water as pods fill and begin to dry. Let the pods rattle dry on the plant before harvesting, and expect the small, dense seeds to cook into a firm-textured, mild bean well suited to the same long-simmered pots used for red kidney beans.
sources: Escuela Agricola Panamericana (Zamorano) Bean Breeding Program
Centro Internacional de Agricultura Tropical (CIAT) Bean Program
Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Bean Variety Catalog
